meta.blurb: Days before his engagement is announced, Prince Felix climbs onto a night train in a borrowed coat and calls himself Fen. By morning he is working in a lakeside bookshop, very badly, for a bookseller who has no idea who he is.
meta.bible: Felix: Crown Prince of Aldoria, twenty-six, polite, clever and never allowed to choose; calls himself Fen in Lindenmere. Fen was the name his late mother used for him when nobody was listening. King Anton: Felix's father, stern, secretly a romantic; his late wife, Felix's mother, once sold apple pies in a market. Livia: Felix's sister, a princess of seventeen, clever and brave. Lady Cecile Marchand: Felix's intended bride, who loves another man, the stable master. Captain Hale: the kind old head of the palace guard. Maren Vos: owner of the Lantern Bookshop, practical and warm; her father opened the shop and has died. Pepper: the shop cat. Mrs Kell: the grumpy baker of Lindenmere who has a good heart. Nina Strand: a newspaper reporter. Aldoria: a mountain kingdom. Halden Palace: the palace in Aldoria. Brinmark: the neighbouring country. Lindenmere: a small lake town in Brinmark. The Lantern Bookshop: the shop with a green door, a debt to the bank due by the end of October. The Night of Lanterns: the book festival by the lake. The Harvest Ball: the court ball where the engagement is to be announced. The Royal Reading Fund: Felix and Livia's plan for village libraries. Added facts: Berta: the palace cook, who helps Felix escape. Tomas Brandt: the stable master Lady Cecile loves. Joss: the boatman of Lindenmere. Mr Ferris: the ironmonger. Miss Pell: the florist. Ada: a small girl at the Saturday story hour. The Lamplighter's Daughter: Maren's father's favourite book; Felix's mother owned a worn copy. Brinmark Gazette: Nina's newspaper. Felix's mother died when he was twelve. The Harvest Ball is six weeks away at the start. Felix lives in Lindenmere about five weeks. Voice and tone: warm, funny and romantic; a gentle comedy of a prince learning to be ordinary, with a happy ending.

A1A2: Prince Felix looked out of the window of his big palace.
Every hour of his day was written on a small card.
Lady Cecile came to tea, and they were both very polite.
Livia loved books, and she wanted a library in every village.
The king called Felix to his office and said the match was settled.
Felix wanted to say no, but the words would not come.
That night Felix remembered his mother, who had called him Fen.
At midnight Livia came to his room and told him to run.
She gave him a plain coat, a cap and a train ticket.
Felix walked quietly through the dark kitchen and out of the palace.
Felix walked to the little station, and nobody knew him.
The night train came in with a loud cloud of steam.
He sat down between a farmer and a woman with wool.
The inspector asked his name, and he said, “Fen.”
An old woman shared her bread and cheese with him.
At the border, an officer waved him into Brinmark.
He wrote the name Fen again and again.
At dawn the train stopped at the end of the line.
At the bakery he paid for a roll with too much money.
He ate his roll by the lake and felt free.
Felix counted his coins and saw that there were few.
He saw a sign: Help Wanted at the Lantern Bookshop.
Inside, a grey cat slept on a pile of books.
A young woman on a tall ladder looked down at him.
Maren asked if he could lift, count and read.
She asked for a letter, but he had none.
A customer came in, and Felix sold her a book.
Maren gave him a one-week trial and a room upstairs.
The stairs were narrow, and the attic room was tiny.
That night Felix slept better than he ever had before.
On his first morning, Felix could not make the tea.
Felix carried the boxes, but the stack fell down.
He did not know how to use the old till.
Felix put the cooking books on the poetry shelf.
A woman asked for help, and Felix chose a book.
Pepper the cat sat on the book Felix was reading.
Mrs Kell came in and knew him at once.
A little girl asked Felix to read her a story.
Maren watched him read and gave him another chance.
At the end of the week, Maren kept him on.
Maren held a letter from the bank in her hand.
The shop must pay the bank by the end of October.
Her father borrowed the money when he was sick.
Felix did not understand money, but he understood her sadness.
Felix promised to help her, and Maren laughed sadly.
Felix burned the supper, and Maren began to laugh.
Maren taught him how to cut an onion for soup.
They ate hot soup and talked about their favourite books.
On Saturday Felix read to a room full of children.
The parents asked if the new man would stay.
At the palace, a servant found the prince's bed empty.
Captain Hale found the kitchen door open and unlocked.
Captain Hale told the king that Felix was gone.
The king ordered a search, but he wanted it secret.
Only Livia sat quietly in the corner with her book.
Lady Cecile heard that Felix was ill, but she doubted it.
A train man remembered a young man named Fen.
When the king heard the name Fen, he was silent.
That night the king stood alone before his wife's picture.
Livia asked the king to give Felix time.
Felix learned fast, and the shelves looked much better.
Felix learned what each regular customer liked to read.
Many price tags in the shop were in her father's writing.
Maren told Felix about her father over evening tea.
Her father opened the shop when she was small.
His favourite book was The Lamplighter's Daughter.
Felix said that his mother had read to him too.
Maren asked about his family, and he answered carefully.
They watched the lamps come on across the lake.
That night Felix knew he had never been happier.
Maren looked at the account book and shook her head.
Felix pointed across the lake and had a big idea.
Maren asked who would come to a night of books.
They drew a plan for the festival on brown paper.
They chose a Saturday for the festival at the end of the month.
Felix drew a bright poster for the festival.
They hung the posters all over the town.
But a hundred paper lanterns cost too much money.
Felix had an idea: the children could make lanterns.
Maren said he bowed like a prince in a play.
Mr Ferris agreed to sell them wire at a low price.
Miss Pell gave them pretty flowers for the stalls.
Joss said he would take the lanterns out in his boat.
The cafe owner offered to sell hot chocolate at the festival.
Only Mrs Kell the baker had not yet answered.
Felix bowed low, and Mrs Kell told him to stand up.
Mrs Kell made Felix carry heavy sacks of flour.
Mrs Kell showed him how to make bread dough.
Mrs Kell said she would bake biscuits for the festival.
Maren asked how he had won Mrs Kell over.
Dark clouds covered the lake, and Maren closed the shop.
Thunder crashed, the lights went out, and Felix lit candles.
They sat together under a blanket while the storm raged.
Maren said she was afraid of losing her father's shop.
Felix told her that he had never been so happy.
Maren asked him who he really was.
Their hands almost touched, but Pepper jumped between them.
Rain dripped through the roof, so they used buckets.
The storm passed, and they went out under the stars.
That night Felix knew he was falling in love.
Felix looked at the account book and found a problem.
Felix drew a plan to help the shop earn more.
Maren asked where he had learned so much.
A reporter came to write about the festival.
Nina took photographs, and Felix hid behind the shelf.
Nina asked Felix where he came from.
Nina said she thought she had seen him before.
Maren told Nina about her father and the shop.
Nina left and promised to write about the festival.
Felix looked at the newspapers, and he felt better.
Livia phoned Felix in the attic late at night.
Livia said that the king was looking for him.
Livia said that Lady Cecile did not want to marry him.
Cecile loved Tomas, the man who looked after the horses.
Livia asked him to come home before the ball.
Felix said he would think about it.
Felix knew he must go home, but he did not want to.
Felix tried to tell Maren, but a customer came in.
Maren was so happy that Felix could not tell her.
Felix decided to tell her the truth after the festival.
The town's children made paper lanterns in the school hall.
Mrs Kell baked hundreds of biscuits shaped like stars.
Joss put a lantern on the lake to test it.
Two musicians played happy music beside the lake.
Felix painted a big sign for the festival night.
They chose the stories that Felix would read aloud.
The whole town helped hang the lanterns on strings.
Nina's story came out in the newspaper.
Maren worried that they did not have enough books.
Felix fell asleep at the table, and Maren covered him.
On festival day, lanterns hung along the whole shore.
Maren and Felix climbed ladders to hang the last lanterns.
They almost kissed, but Mrs Kell shouted from below.
They set up long tables and stacked the books.
At dusk the first visitors came by bus.
The shore filled with people and with lanterns of light.
Maren held Felix's hand tightly in the busy crowd.
Felix climbed on the small stage to read the first story.
Felix read the story in a soft, warm voice.
When he finished, everyone clapped, and Maren cried.
A long line of people waited to buy books.
They ran out of coins, and Mrs Kell helped.
Nina was in the crowd, taking many photographs.
By midnight, the shop had sold nearly every book.
Only a little money was still needed for the bank.
At midnight, hundreds of lanterns floated out on the lake.
The people went home, and they walked to the bridge.
On the little bridge Maren and Felix kissed.
They walked home hand in hand, and Pepper waited.
Felix was happy, but the day of the ball was coming closer.
In the morning Maren asked Felix to stay for good.
Felix wanted to say yes, but he felt very guilty.
Mrs Kell ran across the lane holding a newspaper.
The front page said, The Missing Prince Is Found.
Maren held the newspaper and asked, “Is it true?”
Felix told her everything about himself and his home.
Maren was hurt that he had hidden the truth.
Felix said he was afraid of being only a prince.
Maren asked him to go home and think.
Felix packed his small bag and walked out.
Captain Hale was waiting by a car outside.
Nina came and told Felix that she was sorry.
Mrs Kell gave him a bag of warm bread.
Little Ada gave Felix a small lantern to take home.
Felix looked back at the lanterns as the car drove away.
Hale said the king had not slept since Felix left.
Hale said he knew why Felix chose the name Fen.
Tall mountains rose ahead, and Felix was home again.
At night the car came to the palace gates.
Livia hugged him and said the king would speak in the morning.
In the morning, Felix stood before the king in the great hall.
The king said that the engagement would still go on.
For the first time in his life, Felix said no.
The king sent everyone away and spoke to Felix alone.
Felix said that a prince must be free to choose.
The king said the ball would still happen in a week.
In the library, Felix, Livia and Cecile made a plan.
Cecile spoke happily about Tomas, the man she loved.
Felix wrote a letter to Maren, but it was hard.
He sent the parcel with a rider the next morning.
A small parcel came for Maren from far away.
It was a worn copy of her father's favourite book.
The note said the book was his mother's.
That night Maren read the book and thought of her father.
Maren was still angry, and she told Pepper so.
A card arrived from Princess Livia, inviting Maren to the ball.
Maren almost threw it away, but Mrs Kell stopped her.
Mrs Kell made Maren a beautiful green dress.
Maren took the night train to the mountains in her dress.
Maren arrived at the palace, feeling very nervous.
The ball began, and the king raised his hand.
Lady Cecile stepped forward and spoke before the king could.
Cecile left the hall with the man she loved.
Then Felix stepped forward and said he agreed with Cecile.
He said he would build libraries and marry for love.
Livia clapped first, and then the others began to clap.
Then Felix saw Maren in the doorway, and he ran to her.
Felix told her that he was sorry, and she smiled.
The king watched them and remembered his own wife.
Felix and Maren were happy, and the shop stayed open.
B1B2: Prince Felix of Aldoria stood at a high window and watched the gardeners hang flowers for the Harvest Ball. In six weeks his engagement would be announced to the whole kingdom.
Each morning a servant brought Felix a card that listed every hour of his day. Breakfast, lessons, new clothes and a dinner with ambassadors were all decided long before he woke up.
Lady Cecile came to tea in the garden room, and she and Felix talked kindly about the weather. Whenever she thought he was not looking, she glanced sadly out of the window at the stable yard.
Princess Livia, who was seventeen, sat on the library ladder with a map of Aldoria on her knees. She and Felix had a secret plan to build a small library in every mountain village.
King Anton sent for his son and told him, without looking up from his papers, that the match with Lady Cecile was settled. The engagement would be announced at the Harvest Ball in six weeks.
Felix tried to tell his father that he did not love Cecile and could not marry her. The king only replied that a prince serves his country, and the words died in Felix's throat.
That night Felix stood alone on the balcony and thought of his mother, who had died when he was twelve. She used to call him Fen, and she used to bring him apple pie in secret from the kitchens.
At midnight Livia crept into his bedroom in her dressing gown, holding a candle in her hand. She said that if he stayed he would marry a woman he did not love, so he should go away for a while.
Livia had thought of everything, and she had been planning it for a week. She pressed into his hands a plain coat, a cap, a few coins and a ticket for the night train to Brinmark.
Felix crept down the back stairs and through the sleeping kitchen, where the cook gave him a wink and a warm roll. A moment later the heavy door closed behind him and he was free.
Felix hurried down the hill to the village station with his cap pulled low over his eyes. Not one person on the dark street looked at him twice.
Felix waited on the empty platform, afraid that someone would run out of the dark and drag him home. Then the night train rolled in with a great hiss of steam, and he stepped aboard.
Felix found a seat in a crowded carriage between a snoring farmer and a woman who was knitting a scarf. He had never travelled without guards, a private compartment and a servant to carry his bag.
A tired inspector punched his ticket and asked for his name. Felix opened his mouth to say Felix and, to his own surprise, answered Fen.
An old woman across the aisle noticed that Fen was staring at her basket, and she handed him half a sandwich. He had eaten at banquets all his life, but nothing had ever tasted so good.
In the middle of the night the train stopped at the border, and a sleepy officer looked at the travel card Livia had given him. He stamped it, yawned and welcomed him to Brinmark.
Felix was too excited to sleep, so he took a pencil and wrote the name Fen again and again on the back of his ticket. It looked small and plain and free, and he began to smile.
As morning came, the train ran along the shore of a wide blue lake and stopped at a tiny station. This was Lindenmere, the end of the line, and Felix had no idea what to do next.

The only shop open so early was a bakery, where Felix asked for a roll and held out the biggest note in his pocket. The baker, a large woman with floury arms, asked him very sternly whether he had anything smaller.
Felix sat on a bench by the water and ate the roll slowly while the mist rose from the lake. He was alone, nameless and a little frightened, and he could not remember ever being so happy.
Felix emptied his pockets onto his palm and counted everything he owned in the world. It was not much, and he understood that he would have to find work soon.
At the corner of a quiet lane he found a bookshop with a bright green door and a hand-painted sign in the window. The sign said that the Lantern Bookshop needed an assistant.
Through the window he could see crowded shelves, a warm yellow lamp and a grey cat asleep on a pile of books. It looked like the kindest room in the world.
A bell rang over the door, and a young woman standing on a tall ladder looked down with an armful of books. This was Maren Vos, the owner, and she studied him as though he were a very odd customer.
Maren climbed down and asked whether he could lift boxes, count money and read aloud. Felix answered yes to everything in the voice of an ambassador, which made her raise an eyebrow.
Maren asked who had employed him before and whether he had a letter from anyone at all. Felix said that he came from far away and that his last employer would not write one.
A customer came in looking for a gift, and Felix began to talk about one of his favourite books. She bought it at once, and Maren stopped frowning.
Maren sighed and said that he could have a trial for one week, with the little attic room as part of the pay. If he was lazy or dishonest, he would be gone by Saturday.
Felix climbed three flights of narrow stairs and found an attic room with a slanted ceiling, a small bed and a round window. From the window he could see the whole shining lake.
That night Felix lay in the narrow bed and listened to the water lapping against the shore. Pepper the cat climbed onto his feet, and he slept better than he ever had in the palace.
Maren asked him to make tea, and Felix stared at the kettle as if it were a puzzle from an ancient temple. At the palace a servant had always done it, and nobody had ever shown him how.
Felix tried to carry six boxes of new books at the same time, and the whole tower fell on the floor. Pepper watched from the windowsill with the face of a cat who had seen it all before.
Maren showed him the brass till twice, but Felix pressed the wrong button and the drawer shot open and hit him. He then gave a customer far too much change, and she gladly took it.
Felix was told to put the books back in order, and he put the cookery books in the poetry corner. He explained that both were about making something delicious out of simple things.
A woman asked for a book to read on a long journey, and Felix picked one from a high shelf without hesitating. She came back an hour later to say that she had finished it in the park.
Pepper had decided that Felix was acceptable, and she took to sitting on whatever he was reading. He did not mind, because he had never before been chosen by anyone for no reason at all.

Mrs Kell marched in to buy a book of recipes and recognised the young man who had paid for a roll with an enormous banknote. She told Maren, loudly, that her new assistant had never heard of small change.
A small girl called Ada tugged his sleeve and asked whether he would read her a story. Felix sat down on the floor and began, and soon the whole shop was listening.
Maren watched from behind the counter as Felix read in different voices for every character. When the story ended she said quietly that he could stay until the end of the week.
By Saturday evening Felix had broken a lamp, flooded the kitchen and lost the key to the stockroom twice. Maren looked at him for a long moment and told him that he could stay for another week.
One evening at closing time, Maren stood very still at the counter with a letter in her hand. It was from the bank, and it was not good news.
The letter said that the shop owed the bank a large sum of money. If it was not paid by the end of October, the Lantern Bookshop would be closed and sold.

Maren explained that her father had borrowed money from the bank to repair the roof and to pay for his care when he fell ill. After he died, she kept the shop going alone, but the debt grew faster than the sales.
Felix had never owed money to anyone, for the palace had always paid for everything. Yet he understood perfectly well what it means to love a place and be afraid of losing it.
Felix said that he would do everything he could to help save the shop. Maren laughed and reminded him that he had once flooded the kitchen with a single kettle.
That evening Felix offered to make supper and burned a whole loaf of bread under the grill. Smoke filled the room, the alarm began to shriek, and Maren laughed so hard that she had to sit down.

Maren opened the window and handed him a knife and an onion, and she showed him how to chop it. His eyes streamed with tears, and she told him that this was the only cooking lesson that really mattered.
They ate the soup at the counter, which was crowded with books and covered in crumbs. They talked for hours about their favourite stories, and neither of them noticed that it was midnight.
On Saturday morning the shop held its story hour, and the children sat in a ring on cushions. Felix read in a different voice for every character, and the children laughed until they fell over.
The parents crowded around Maren after the story and asked whether the new assistant was staying. She glanced at Felix, who was surrounded by children, and said that he was staying for now.
At Halden Palace the valet carried in the morning tray and found the prince's bed untouched. The window was open, the coat was gone from its hook, and a single card lay on the pillow.
Captain Hale searched the palace from the cellars to the roof and found the kitchen door unlocked. Berta the cook said that she had been asleep all night and had seen nothing at all.
Captain Hale stood in front of the king's desk and reported, with great reluctance, that the prince had vanished in the night. King Anton did not speak for a long moment.
King Anton, white with anger and something that looked like fear, ordered a search at once. He insisted that it be kept secret from the newspapers and from the court.
Only Livia sat calmly in a corner of the room, turning the pages of a book she was not reading. When the king glared at her, she said that she knew nothing and was very worried.
A courtier told Lady Cecile that the prince was unwell and could not see visitors for a few days. She smiled politely, looked across the hall at Livia, and was almost certain that it was not true.

Captain Hale sent his most trusted men to every station, and one of them found a tired inspector with a magnificent moustache. The inspector remembered a thin young man who had said that his name was Fen.
When Captain Hale told the king about the name, King Anton went very still and turned his face away. It had been years since he had heard the name Fen spoken aloud.
That night King Anton walked alone down the long gallery to the portrait of his late wife. He stood there for a long time, and the guards pretended not to see his face.
Livia knocked at the study door and quietly asked her father to give Felix some time. The king replied that the ball would go on whatever happened, and she saw that he was afraid.
As the days went by, Felix learned where everything belonged, and the shelves began to look tidy and inviting. Maren noticed it with some surprise, although she never said so aloud.

Felix learned that the old doctor liked poems, the baker's son loved sea stories and the schoolteacher read nothing but mysteries. Soon he could find the right book for each of them before they asked.
One afternoon Felix noticed that half of the price tags in the shop were written in an old, careful hand. Maren said that they were her father's, and that she could not bring herself to replace them.
At dusk they sat on the shop steps with mugs of tea and watched the lamps come on along the lake. Maren said that her father had read to her every single night until she was twelve.

Maren's father had opened the Lantern Bookshop when she was a small girl, and he had named it after his favourite story. He had wanted a place where anyone, rich or poor, could come in and find something to love.
His favourite book was a story called The Lamplighter's Daughter, about a girl who lit the lamps of a harbour town. He had read it to her so many times that the cover had come away.
Felix was quiet for a while, and then he said that his own mother had read to him as well. She had died when he was twelve, and he had never told anyone how much he missed it.
Maren asked gently where his family lived and what they did. Felix said that they were a large, formal and very strict family who lived far away in the mountains.
They watched the last light fade from the sky as the lamps came on around the shore. For a while neither of them spoke, and the silence felt warm and easy.
Back in the attic, Felix leaned out of the round window and looked at the stars over the lake. He was happier than he had ever been, and it frightened him.
Late one night Maren sat over the account book with a pencil and a very long face. No matter how she added the numbers, ordinary sales would never pay the bank in time.
Felix looked out at the dark lake and had an idea. He suggested a festival at night, with books on tables along the shore and hundreds of lanterns shining on the water.
Maren asked who in the world would come to a village on a cold night to buy books. Felix answered that books at night are like stories by a fire, and that people always want to come in.
Over the next few evenings they drew the plan together on a long sheet of brown paper. It had tables for books, a stage for readings and a hundred lanterns to float on the lake.
Maren counted the days and chose a Saturday near the end of the month for the festival. That left only a few weeks to do an enormous amount of work.
Felix took a brush and drew a poster of the lake covered in glowing lanterns, with an open book in the middle. Maren stared at it, amazed, and asked where he had learned to paint like that.
Maren had two hundred copies printed at the copy shop by the station. They spent a whole afternoon pinning posters to lamp posts, fences and the doors of every shop in town.
A day later the price list for the paper lanterns arrived, and it was far higher than Maren had hoped. She sat down on a stool and said that the festival was already over before it had begun.
Felix had another idea, and this time it was cheap. If the children made the lanterns themselves at the Saturday story hour, they would need only paper, string and glue.
Felix bowed low to thank her, and Maren laughed and said that he bowed like a prince in a play. He laughed much too loudly, and she gave him a puzzled look.
Their first visit was to Mr Ferris, who sold nails, wire and paper at the corner of the square. After hearing the plan, he said that he would sell them the wire at half the price.
Miss Pell, the florist, was next, and she promised to decorate every stall with autumn flowers. She added that she had always thought the town needed something beautiful to happen to it.
Joss owned a fleet of small rowing boats, and he said that he would gladly float the lanterns out on the water at midnight. He had never seen a festival on the lake, and he liked the idea at once.
The owner of the little cafe on the square offered to run a hot chocolate stall by the shore. She said that nobody in the world could resist hot chocolate on a cold night beside water.
Only one shop remained, and it was the one they were most afraid to enter. Mrs Kell the baker had a reputation for turning away anyone who asked her for anything at all.
Felix gave Mrs Kell his deepest and most elegant bow, the one he had been taught for visiting kings. She told him to stand up straight and asked whether he thought she was a duke.
Mrs Kell said that if he wanted her help he would have to earn it by carrying flour at five in the morning. For three mornings in a row, Felix did exactly that.
On the third morning Mrs Kell grudgingly taught him how to knead the dough. He was clumsy, but he did not complain, and she gave a small grunt of approval.
At last Mrs Kell agreed to bake star-shaped biscuits for every visitor. She added gruffly that she had known Maren's father, and that he had always paid his bills on time.
Back at the shop Maren asked him how on earth he had won over the most difficult woman in Lindenmere. Felix said that it had taken three mornings and a great deal of flour.
One evening heavy black clouds rolled across the lake, and the wind began to howl in the chimney. Maren closed the shop early and told Felix to come in from the street.
A great crack of thunder shook the building, and every light in the shop went out at once. Felix felt for matches and lit all the candles he could find, and the room glowed softly.
They sat on the floor behind the counter and shared a blanket while the rain drummed on the windows. Maren made a flask of tea, and Pepper climbed down to hide between them.
Maren confessed that she was frightened of losing the shop. It was the only place in the world where she could still feel her father near her.
Felix said that he had never been so happy in his whole life as he had been in her shop. He said that it was not the books but the people in it that made it so.
Maren looked at him closely in the flickering light and asked who he really was. Felix thought for a long moment and said that he was someone who wanted very much to be there.
Their hands moved closer together on the blanket until they were almost touching. At that moment Pepper leaped between them with a yowl, and both of them jumped.

Suddenly Maren pointed at the ceiling, where rain was dripping steadily onto the stack of atlases. They ran for buckets and saucepans and set them all around the shop, and the rain played a tune on them.
Near midnight the storm blew away across the mountains, and the clouds opened to show a sky full of stars. They stepped out onto the wet cobbles and stood together by the lake.
Up in the attic Felix lay awake and listened to the drip of the roof. He knew now that he was falling in love, and he knew that he had not told her the truth.
Felix had been trained to read the budgets of an entire kingdom, so one small shop was no trouble at all. He soon found that the shop lost money on every old book it sold for a discount.
Felix drew a plan on a clean sheet of paper with arrows and little boxes. It suggested a corner for second-hand books, gift wrapping at the counter and kits for making lanterns.
Maren stared at the plan and asked where on earth he had learned to do such things. Felix said that he had had a tutor who was very dull, but who had been extremely thorough.
A newspaper reporter named Nina Strand arrived from the city to write about the festival. She had seen the poster at the railway station and thought that it looked wonderful.
Nina photographed the shop, the lake and the cheerful new assistant, who tried to hide behind a rack of postcards. He only succeeded in knocking it over, and she took a picture of that too.
Nina asked Felix where he came from, how long he had lived in Lindenmere and what he had done before. His answers were polite and friendly, but they did not tell her anything at all.
Nina looked at him a little longer than seemed polite, as though she were trying to remember something. She asked whether they had met, and Felix said quickly that he had one of those faces.
When Nina interviewed Maren, she spoke about her father and the shop that he had built. The reporter put down her pencil, because she was too moved to write.
Nina said goodbye at the door and promised that her article would appear in the Brinmark Gazette within the week. Felix waved cheerfully, but a cold feeling crept into his stomach.
The next morning Felix hurried to the station kiosk and searched every newspaper for news of a missing prince. There was nothing at all, and he understood that his father was keeping the secret.

Maren almost threw the card into the stove, but Mrs Kell, who had read it over her shoulder, told her that she was going. She said that nobody should miss the end of a story.

Captain Hale met her at the station with a car, and he bowed as though she were a duchess. When they reached the palace, Livia led her to a quiet corner by the ballroom doors.
The Harvest Ball glittered in the Hall of Mirrors, where hundreds of dancers swirled under glowing chandeliers. At the height of the music, King Anton raised his hand, and the room fell silent.
