Felix drew himself up to his full height and declared that he would do everything in his power to help save the shop, in the exact tone he used for official promises. Maren laughed until she had to wipe her eyes again, and she reminded him gently that he had once managed to flood a kitchen with a single kettle. Nevertheless, she admitted, with a small and rueful smile, it was very nice to hear somebody say such a thing aloud.

That evening Felix insisted on making supper to thank her, and he set a whole loaf of bread under the grill and wandered off to look for a plate. Within moments the kitchen filled with black smoke, the alarm began to shriek and Pepper fled upstairs, while Maren leaned against the wall and laughed until she could hardly breathe. It was the first time he had heard her laugh properly, and he decided that it was worth the loss of a loaf.

Maren flung open the window to clear the smoke, handed him a small knife and an onion and showed him how to chop it into neat little squares. Within a minute his eyes were streaming, and he was weeping over the board like a tragic hero, while she told him that this was the part of cooking nobody could teach. By the time the soup began to simmer, the kitchen smelled of thyme and he was proud of himself.

They ate the soup at the counter, squeezed between a stack of atlases and a lopsided pile of detective novels, and discovered that they had been reading the same stories all their lives in different cities. Felix confessed that he knew every adventure ever written for children, and Maren admitted that she cried at the end of every one. Neither of them noticed that the church bell had struck midnight, and then struck again for the half hour.

On Saturday morning the shop held its weekly story hour, and a ring of children sat on cushions at Felix's feet with their mouths open in expectation. He read them the story of a dragon who was afraid of the dark, giving the dragon a deep rumble and the dark a terrifying whisper, and they shrieked with joy at every page. When he finished, little Ada demanded, with the authority of a small queen, that he start again from the very beginning.

The parents crowded around Maren after the story, praising the new assistant and asking, with unmistakable hope, whether he planned to stay in Lindenmere. She glanced across the shop at Felix, who was buried under a pile of children and looking happier than any prince had a right to be, and said that he was staying for now. The words were small and casual, but they sounded in her own ears much larger than she had ever meant them to be.

At Halden Palace the valet carried in the morning tray as he had done every day for ten years, and found the prince's enormous bed neatly made and quite untouched. The window stood open, one coat was missing from its hook and the daily card of engagements lay on the pillow, torn carefully in half. He stood there with the tray trembling in his hands, wondering how one announces such a thing to a king.

Captain Hale searched the palace from the cellars to the roof, and at last he knelt beside the kitchen door, which was unlocked and still faintly warm from the stove. Berta the cook declared with enormous firmness that she had slept like a log all night and had seen nothing whatever, and a suspicious number of rolls were missing from her basket. The captain, who had known Felix since he was a child, found that he could not quite bring himself to be angry.

Captain Hale stood before the king's great desk, cap in hand, and reported with obvious reluctance that the prince had vanished in the night and could not be found anywhere in the palace. King Anton did not speak for a very long time, and when he did, his voice was so quiet that the captain had to lean forward to hear it. It was far more frightening, in the captain's long experience, than any shout or thunderclap could possibly have been.

King Anton, white with anger and something that looked suspiciously like fear, ordered a search at once, but he insisted that it be kept secret from the newspapers and the court. A missing crown prince six weeks before the Harvest Ball would be a scandal that no treaty could mend. Nobody in the room dared to point out that the king's voice shook as he gave the order.

Only Livia sat calmly in a velvet chair in the corner of the room, turning the pages of a book that she was plainly not reading. When the king turned his glare upon her, she answered that she knew nothing at all and that she was extremely worried, in the sweet and innocent voice of someone who had rehearsed it before the mirror. The king narrowed his eyes and drew breath to reply, but, for once in his long reign, he found that he had nothing at all to say.

A courtier informed Lady Cecile, with a bow and a very bad smile, that the prince was unwell and unable to receive visitors for several days. She thanked him gracefully, glanced across the hall at Livia, who gave the smallest nod in the history of nodding, and understood at once what had happened. For the first time in weeks, she had to hide a smile behind her fan.

Captain Hale sent his most trusted men, in plain clothes, to every station along the border line, and one of them at last found a tired inspector with a magnificent moustache. The inspector remembered a thin young man in a brown coat who had given the name Fen and then looked as if he had surprised himself. The report reached the palace by evening, and the captain read it with a very strange expression.

When Captain Hale gave him the report, King Anton read the single word at the bottom of the page and turned very slowly toward the window. It had been fourteen years since anyone had spoken that name in his hearing, and it had belonged to a small boy and the queen who loved him. The captain, discreet as always, pretended to study a painting until the king had composed himself.

That night King Anton walked alone down the long portrait gallery until he reached a painting of a smiling woman in a simple blue dress, who had refused to let the court painters make her look more regal. He stood before it for a very long time, with his hands clasped behind his back and his stern face unguarded. The guards at the end of the hall studied the ceiling and pretended not to see.

Livia knocked at the door of the study, walked in without waiting for an answer and quietly asked her father to give Felix a little time. The king replied, without raising his eyes, that the Harvest Ball would go on whatever happened and that a prince could not simply disappear. She saw for the first time that his stiff, stern back was the back of a frightened man.

As the days went by, Felix learned where every book belonged, and the cluttered shelves began to look tidy, welcoming and almost deliberate. Maren noticed the change with some surprise, though she took care never to say so aloud, in case it went to his head. She did, however, quietly stop checking his work every hour, and then every other hour, and finally not at all.

Felix learned that the retired doctor loved poetry, that the baker's son devoured stories of the sea and that the schoolteacher read nothing but mysteries and pretended that she did not. Within a fortnight he could put the right book into a customer's hands before the customer had finished asking. Maren confessed, with a catch in her voice, that her father had possessed exactly the same gift and had used it just as kindly.

One afternoon Felix noticed that half of the price tags tucked into the old books were written in a spidery, careful hand that did not belong to Maren. She told him quietly that they were her father's, that he had written them every winter for thirty years, and that she could not bring herself to throw a single one away. Felix put the old book back on the shelf with great gentleness, as though it were something alive and easily frightened.

At dusk they sat side by side on the shop steps with mugs of tea and watched the lamps flicker on, one by one, along the dark curve of the lake. Maren said, almost to herself, that her father had read to her every night of her childhood, long after she was old enough to read for herself. She had never told that to a stranger before, and she was not sure why she was telling it now.

Maren's father had opened the Lantern Bookshop when she was a small girl, with a loan, a borrowed ladder and a cart of secondhand books, and he had named it after his favourite story. He had wanted a place where anyone, rich or poor, could come in out of the rain and find a book to love. The sign above the door, she said, was the only thing he had ever painted himself.

His favourite book was a story called The Lamplighter's Daughter, about a girl who climbs the hills every evening to light the lamps of a harbour town and finds that the whole town depends on her. He had read it aloud to Maren so many times that the cover had fallen away and had to be mended with tape. She no longer owned a copy, because it had gone to the bank with everything else that could be sold.

Felix was quiet for a while, watching a single boat cross the dark water, and then he said that his own mother had read to him in the same way. She had died when he was twelve, he added, and in all the years since he had never told anyone how much he missed the sound of her voice. It was the truest thing he had said in Lindenmere, and it was strangely easy.

Maren asked gently where his family lived, and what sort of people they were, and Felix chose his words with the care of someone crossing a frozen river. He told her that they were a large, formal and very strict family who lived far away in the mountains and who expected a great deal of him. Every word was perfectly true, and yet he felt like a thief who had been caught with his pockets full of her trust.

They watched the last light drain from the sky while the lamps came on one by one around the shore, until the whole lake was circled by a necklace of small gold flames. For a long while neither of them spoke, and the silence was warm and comfortable, the sort that exists only between people who need no explanations. Pepper, who disapproved of silence unless she was the cause of it, settled warmly across both of their feet and began to purr.

Back in the attic, Felix leaned out of the round window and gazed at the stars scattered across the black mirror of the lake. He was happier than he had ever been in his life, and the happiness frightened him a little, because it rested on a name that was not his own. He knew that a day would come when he would have to pay for it.

Late one night Maren sat hunched over the account book with a pencil between her teeth and an expression of deepening gloom. However she added the columns, and she added them four different ways, ordinary sales would never raise enough to satisfy the bank before the end of October. What the shop needed, she said to the cat, was nothing short of a miracle.

Felix, who had been polishing the window, looked out at the dark lake glittering beyond the glass and was struck by an idea so large that he forgot the cloth in his hand. He suggested a festival at night, with books sold from tables along the shore and hundreds of paper lanterns glowing above the water, like a market in a fairy tale. He recalled that his mother had once taken him to a lantern fair and that it had been the happiest night of his boyhood.

Maren pointed out, quite reasonably, that Lindenmere was a small town at the end of a railway line and that nobody in their right mind would cross the country on a cold October night to buy books. Felix answered that a book read by lantern light has a kind of magic that daylight cannot give, and that people are always hungry for magic. She said that it was the silliest idea she had ever heard, and she did not stop thinking about it all night.

Over the next few evenings the two of them drew the plan together on a long sheet of brown paper pinned across the counter, arguing happily over every line. There would be tables of books along the shore, a small stage for readings, a stall for hot chocolate and a hundred lanterns to be floated out upon the water at midnight. By the end of the week the paper was covered in coffee rings, and it looked like a real thing.

Maren counted the days on the calendar twice, circled a Saturday near the end of October in red pencil and announced, with the air of a general planning a campaign, that the festival would take place that night. It left only a few weeks in which to do an enormous amount of work, and it left the bank very little time to wait. Felix said that he had always worked best under pressure, which was not true at all.

Felix took a brush and a pot of ink and, within an hour, produced a poster of the lake covered in floating lanterns, with a great open book rising from the water like a sun. Maren stared at it for a long moment, amazed, and demanded to know where on earth he had learned to paint like that. He said that he had had a very expensive and exceedingly dull art teacher.

Maren took the poster to the little copy shop by the station and ordered two hundred copies, which cost more than she could afford and less than she feared. They spent a whole afternoon pinning posters to lamp posts, fences and shop doors, and Felix hung one upside down and had to be told about it by three different people. By evening, from every corner and every lamp post, the whole of Lindenmere seemed to be shouting the news of the festival.

A day later the price list for the paper lanterns arrived from the city, and the total was far higher than anything Maren had dared to imagine. She sat down heavily on a stool and announced that the festival was finished before it had begun, and the poster on the wall looked down on her sadly. Felix, who had never in his life counted the cost of anything, felt a sudden wish to give her the moon.

Felix had a second idea, and this one cost almost nothing, which delighted them both. If the children folded and painted the lanterns themselves at the Saturday story hour, they would need only paper, string and glue, and every family in town would have a reason to come to the festival. Maren looked at him for a long moment as though he had just invented the wheel.

Felix swept her a deep, elegant bow to thank her for her trust, and Maren burst out laughing and said that he bowed like a prince in a play. He laughed too, much too loudly and for much too long, and she gave him a puzzled sidelong look that he pretended not to see. It occurred to him, with a sinking feeling that was almost a joke, that he would never make a very good criminal.

Their first visit was to Mr Ferris, the ironmonger, who sold nails, rope, wire and paper from a shop so crowded that customers had to enter sideways. He listened to the whole plan with his hands behind his back, muttered a good deal, and then announced that he would supply the wire for the lanterns at half the usual price. Felix thanked him so warmly that the old man blushed to the roots of his hair.

Miss Pell, the florist, was next, and she listened with shining eyes before promising to decorate every stall along the shore with autumn flowers and trailing ivy. She added, rather shyly, that she had always thought that Lindenmere needed something truly beautiful to happen to it, and that she would be honoured to help. They left her shop with an armful of chrysanthemums, a promise of ivy and a loyal new friend.

Joss, the boatman, who owned a small fleet of battered rowing boats and the stoutest pair of arms in Lindenmere, said that he would gladly carry the lanterns out onto the water at midnight and set them adrift. He had never seen a festival on the lake in all his sixty years, and the idea pleased him so much that he refused to accept a penny. Felix suspected, as he shook the old man's enormous hand, that he had just found an ally for life.

The owner of the little cafe on the square, a round and cheerful woman with flour on her apron, offered to run a hot chocolate stall beside the water on the night of the festival. She declared that nobody on earth could resist a steaming mug on a cold night, and that she intended to sell several hundred. Maren wrote it down in her notebook with a hand that was beginning to shake with hope.

Only one shop remained, and it was the one they were both most afraid to enter, for Mrs Kell the baker had a reputation for sending away anyone who dared to ask her for a favour. She had been known to refuse a bishop, a mayor and a travelling circus, all in the same week. Maren straightened her coat, took a deep breath and said that it was only fair to ask her as well.

Felix, who had been trained since childhood to greet royalty, gave Mrs Kell his deepest and most elegant bow, the one that was reserved for visiting kings and archbishops. She stared down at him with her floury arms crossed and told him to stand up straight at once and stop making a fool of himself, since she was neither a duke nor a duchess. Maren, standing behind him in the doorway, pressed a hand over her mouth and trembled with silent laughter.

Mrs Kell said that she never gave anything for nothing, and that if the boy wished for her help he would have to earn it by carrying her sacks of flour at five o'clock in the morning. Felix, who had never in his life risen before the sun without a servant to wake him, appeared on the doorstep at the appointed time on three mornings running. His arms ached for a week, and he would not have admitted it for a kingdom.

On the third morning Mrs Kell, with a great show of reluctance, showed him how to knead a mass of dough until it was smooth and springy. He was clumsy and flour clung to his eyebrows, but he did not complain once, and she gave a small grunt that, from her, was practically a standing ovation. By the time the first loaves came out of the oven, something in her face had begun to thaw.

At last Mrs Kell announced that she would bake star-shaped biscuits for every visitor to the festival, at no cost to anybody, and that nobody was to make a fuss about it. She added gruffly that she had known Maren's father for thirty years, that he had never once been late with his bills, and that he would have been proud. Maren had to turn away suddenly and study a tray of buns to hide the tears that had sprung into her eyes.

Back at the shop Maren folded her arms and demanded to know how on earth he had won over the most difficult woman in the whole of Lindenmere, a task that had defeated three mayors. Felix explained, with a modest shrug, that it had taken three mornings, a very large quantity of flour and an unshakeable refusal to give up. She looked at him with a new and thoughtful expression that made his heart do something peculiar.

One evening heavy black clouds rolled across the lake like an army, and the wind began to howl in the chimney and rattle every shutter in the lane. Maren closed the shop early, turned the sign on the green door and called Felix inside before the first drops fell. Pepper had already retired to the highest shelf, where she sat watching the sky with deep suspicion.

A tremendous crack of thunder shook the whole building to its foundations, and every light in the shop went out at once, leaving them in a pitch dark that smelled of paper and rain. Felix felt his way to the counter, found the matches and lit every candle he could lay his hands on, until the shelves danced with a hundred trembling shadows. The shop had never, in all its crooked and dusty life, looked so beautiful as it did that night in the storm.

They sat on the floor behind the counter, wrapped in a single patchwork blanket, while the rain drummed against the windows and the wind moaned in the chimney like a ghost with a grievance. Maren poured tea from a flask, and Pepper, who had come down from the shelf after all, wedged herself between them with an air of cold superiority. For a long while there was nothing to do but sit together and listen to the weather doing its worst.

Maren hugged her knees and confessed, in a voice so low that Felix could hardly hear it above the rain, that she was frightened of losing the shop. It was the last place on earth where she could still feel her father close to her, in the smell of the paper and the sound of the bell, and she did not know who she would be without it. Felix wished that he could carry her fear for her, if only for an hour.

Felix said, slowly and carefully, as if each word were a step on thin ice, that he had never been so happy in his whole life as he had been in her little shop. It was not the books, he said, though he loved the books, nor the lake or the town, but the person who sat beside him in the candlelight and made all of it matter. It was the second truest thing he had said, and it was a great deal harder than the first.

Maren turned her head and studied him closely in the flickering light, as though she were reading a page in a language she half remembered, and asked quietly who he really was. Felix thought for a long moment, with his heart pounding, and said that he was somebody who wanted very much to be there, in that room, on that night. It was not an answer, and she seemed to know it, but she let it stand.

Their hands crept closer together on the patchwork blanket, an inch at a time, until the space between them was so small that Felix could feel the warmth of her fingers. At that precise moment a flash of lightning lit the room, and Pepper leaped between them with a yowl of outrage and landed on the pile of cushions. They both jumped, and then they began to laugh, helplessly, until the thunder had passed.

Suddenly Maren pointed up at the ceiling, where a dark stain was spreading above the shelf of atlases and a steady drip had begun to fall upon the oldest and most valuable books in the shop. They rushed about with buckets, saucepans and a very large teapot, setting them in a ring on the floorboards, and the rain played a ridiculous little tune upon every one. Maren said that her father had always sworn the roof would be mended next spring.

Near midnight the storm blew itself out over the mountains, the clouds tore open and a sky crowded with stars appeared above the glistening roofs of Lindenmere. They stepped out onto the wet cobbles and stood together by the water, breathing in the cold, clean air, while the last drops fell from the eaves like slow music. Neither of them could think of a single thing to say, and neither of them minded.

Up in the attic Felix lay awake for hours, listening to the last drops tapping on the roof and watching the shadows of the rafters move across the ceiling. He knew now, beyond any doubt, that he was falling in love with Maren Vos, and he knew with equal certainty that she did not even know his name. It was a very strange thing to find himself caught between the happiest and the most shameful night of his life.

Felix, who had been trained from the age of ten to read the budgets of an entire kingdom, found that the accounts of one small bookshop held no terrors for him at all. Within an hour he had discovered that the shop was losing a little money on every old book it sold at a discount, and that the supplier had been charging for delivery twice. Maren looked over his shoulder at the columns of figures with her mouth slightly open, and for once she had no answer ready.

Felix drew a plan on a clean sheet of paper, with arrows and neat little boxes that spread across the page like the branches of a tree. It suggested a corner for secondhand books, a gift-wrapping service at the counter and lantern-making kits that families could buy and take home to build. Every item was small and sensible, and together they added up to a future.

Maren stared at the plan for a long time and asked where on earth a travelling assistant had learned to understand accounts like that. Felix said carefully that he had once had a tutor who was exceedingly dull but extremely thorough, and that some of it had stuck. She narrowed her eyes, and he recalled that he must be careful, because she noticed everything.

A newspaper reporter named Nina Strand arrived from the city one bright morning to write a short piece about the festival, a notebook in one hand and a camera hanging from her neck. She had seen one of the posters pinned up at the railway station, she said, and it had been the only cheerful thing she had seen all week. Maren, flattered and a little nervous, offered her the best chair in the shop and a cup of tea in the good cup.

Nina photographed the shop, the lake and the cheerful new assistant, who tried to hide behind a rack of postcards and succeeded only in knocking it over with a crash. She caught the whole moment on film, the flying postcards, the rolling cat and the prince's crimson face, and she laughed so kindly that he almost forgave her. He did not yet know how much trouble that single photograph was going to cause him before the month was over.

Nina asked Felix where he came from, how long he had lived in Lindenmere and what he had done before he came to work in a bookshop. His answers were polite and charming and entirely empty, like beautifully wrapped boxes with nothing inside, and the reporter's pencil moved more slowly each time. She had interviewed politicians for years, and she knew a smooth answer when she heard one.

Nina looked at him a little longer than seemed polite, her head tilted to one side, as though she were trying to remember something that lay just out of reach. She asked whether they had ever met before, perhaps at a newspaper office or a public event in the city, and Felix said quickly that he had one of those faces that everyone thought they knew. It was an explanation that satisfied nobody in the room, and least of all the young man who was giving it.

When Nina turned to interview Maren, the answers came so easily and so warmly that the reporter forgot to take notes. She heard about the loan, the leaking roof, the old price tags and the father who had read aloud to his daughter every night, and by the end Nina's own eyes were suspiciously bright. It was, she told herself, the best story she had been given in years.

Nina shook hands with them both at the green door and promised that her article would appear in the Brinmark Gazette within the week, with photographs. Felix waved cheerfully until she had turned the corner, and then he sat down on the nearest chair, as a cold feeling spread through his stomach. A reporter's camera, it occurred to him, was a very dangerous kind of mirror.

The next morning Felix hurried to the station kiosk and searched every newspaper on the rack for news of a missing prince, his heart in his mouth. There was not a word, not even a whisper in the gossip column, and he understood at last that his father, for reasons of pride or of fear, was keeping the secret. He bought a bar of chocolate with his change and ate it on the way home.

One night a small phone that Livia had hidden in the lining of the coat began to buzz urgently against the attic floorboards, and Felix, who had almost forgotten that it existed, snatched it up with trembling fingers. His sister's voice came through a hiss of static, small and bright and astonishingly close. He sat down heavily on the narrow bed and closed his eyes to listen, as though the words might be easier to hold that way.

Livia told him in a low, rapid voice that the king had sent men to every station along the border and that Captain Hale himself was already travelling quietly toward Brinmark. She said that the captain was kind and clever and unhurried, and that he would find his prince in a week or so whatever anyone did. The news fell on Felix like a cold hand laid suddenly upon his shoulder, and the little attic seemed to shrink around him.

Livia then told him the strangest news of all, which was that Lady Cecile Marchand did not wish to marry him either, and had been quietly hoping for a way out since the very first day. She was waiting for someone to be brave enough to speak first, and Livia was quite certain that this someone ought to be the prince. Felix burst out laughing and had to press the pillow to his face to keep the whole house from hearing his delight.

Livia explained that Cecile had loved Tomas Brandt, the stable master, since they were both children, and that he loved her with the whole of his honest heart. She could not refuse the king herself without bringing disgrace upon her family, but if the prince spoke first, the court would have to listen. Felix recalled the sad glances at the stable yard and felt like the greatest fool in Aldoria.

Livia begged him to come home before the night of the Harvest Ball, because he was the only person who could stand up in front of the court and stop the engagement. Without him, she said, Cecile would be married to the wrong man, and she would never have the chance to build her libraries. Her voice wavered on the last words, and he remembered with a pang of guilt that she was only seventeen and carrying all of this alone.

Felix said, in a voice that sounded hollow and strange even to himself, that he needed time to think, and Livia, who knew her brother's habits of mind exceedingly well, did not argue with him. She gave him until the end of the festival and promised to call again on the evening before the ball. He hung up and sat for a long time with the dead phone in his hand.

Felix stood at the round window and stared down at the dark lake, torn in two by feelings that would not be reconciled. He knew that he owed his sister, his country and Cecile the courage to go home, and he knew with equal certainty that he could not bear to leave Maren and the festival that they had built together. He had never realised before that duty and happiness could weigh exactly the same.

The next morning Felix resolved to tell Maren everything, and he waited until the shop was empty, took a deep breath and opened his mouth to begin. At that precise moment the bell over the door jangled and a customer bustled in asking for a map of the northern lakes, followed by two friends and a dog. By the time the shop was quiet again, he had lost his nerve completely.

That afternoon he tried a second time, but Maren was humming to herself as she wrote a long list of preparations for the festival, and her face was brighter than he had ever seen it. She was so full of hope and so busy with happiness that he simply could not find it in himself to break the spell. He put the truth back in his pocket, where it grew heavier by the hour.

In the end, lying awake at three in the morning, he made a solemn promise to himself that he would stay until the festival was over and the shop was safe. Then he would tell Maren the whole truth, go home to face his father and trust that she would understand. It was a sensible plan, and like most sensible plans made at three in the morning, it was too good to be true.

Every afternoon after lessons the children of Lindenmere gathered at long tables in the school hall to cut, fold and paint paper lanterns in every colour imaginable. Felix moved from table to table with his sleeves rolled up, steadying scissors, rescuing fingers from glue and telling terrible jokes that were rewarded with shrieks of laughter. By the end of the first week there were two hundred lanterns drying on the windowsills.

Mrs Kell filled her bakery with the warm smell of ginger and butter as she cut and baked hundreds of star-shaped biscuits for the festival, working from before dawn until the shop windows steamed over. She went on insisting that it was nothing at all and that nobody should dare to thank her, and she blushed furiously whenever anyone did. Felix, who was allowed to taste the failures, thought that she was the finest baker in the world.

Joss rowed out onto the lake one windless evening to test the floating lanterns that Felix had designed with a great deal of confidence and no previous experience. The first one sank like a stone, the second caught fire and had to be put out with a bucket, but the third drifted away across the water, glowing like a tiny golden ship. The whole shore cheered at the sight, and Joss stood up in his wobbling boat and took a very deep bow.

An old fiddler and a young woman with an accordion began to practise on a bench beside the lake each evening, and the music they made was part lullaby, part dance and altogether irresistible. It drifted over the water and into the open windows of the town, and people stopped in the street with their shopping bags to listen. Maren decided on the spot that the festival would have a ballroom floor made of cobblestones.

Felix painted the shop windows with golden stars and wrote the words Night of Lanterns in swirling, curling letters on a long wooden board that Mr Ferris had found for him. When the paint dried, Maren stood in the lane with her hands on her hips and declared that it was the most beautiful sign in the whole of Brinmark. Felix tried very hard to look modest, as a gentleman should, and failed completely in front of everyone.

Maren and Felix argued cheerfully for an entire evening about which stories ought to be read aloud on the night of the festival. She wanted a quiet old tale about a lighthouse keeper and the sea, while he wanted something with a dragon in it, and they might have gone on until dawn if Pepper had not walked across the list. In the end they chose both, with the lighthouse first, because the shore would be dark and still.

On the Thursday before the festival, the whole town came out into the lane with ladders, string and mugs of tea to hang the paper lanterns in long glowing loops from roof to roof. Mr Ferris supplied the wire, Miss Pell wound ivy around every post, and even Mrs Kell stood on a stool tying knots while scolding anyone who dared to thank her. By the time the sun went down, the whole lane looked like the inside of a jewel box, glowing and shimmering.

Nina's article appeared in the Brinmark Gazette on Wednesday morning, and it was warmer, funnier and far more generous than Maren had ever dared to hope. By Friday the telephone in the shop was ringing every few minutes with callers asking about trains, and a coach company in the city had announced that it would run two extra buses to Lindenmere. Maren read the article eleven times that day, and she cried a little at the end of every single reading.

Maren was suddenly afraid that the shop would not have enough books for such a large crowd, and she sat down at the counter and counted her savings with a face like a stone. After a long conversation in whispers, she and Felix emptied every tin and jar they could find and telephoned the supplier to order two hundred more. It was a dangerous gamble with the last of her money, and they both knew very well that it could ruin her.

On the night before the festival they worked late among the paper, the string and the glue, long after every other window in the lane had gone dark. Felix fell asleep at last with his head on his folded arms and a half-finished lantern beneath his cheek, and Maren, watching him for a long moment, quietly spread her coat over his shoulders. She turned out the lamp and stood in the doorway until she was certain that he was warm.

On the morning of the festival the whole shore was ready, with paper lanterns hanging from every tree and every lamp post and ribbons fluttering along the railings in the cold clear air. The lake lay as smooth as glass, and the sky above the mountains promised an evening without wind or rain. Maren, who had slept for only three hours, stood at the window and laughed like a child.

In the late afternoon Maren and Felix climbed two ladders side by side to hang the last lanterns over the little wooden bridge, the final touch to a month of labour. As they stretched across the gap to tie the last string, their faces came suddenly very close together, so close that he could count the tiny freckles on her nose. Neither of them moved or spoke, and for one long moment the whole lake seemed to hold its breath beside them.

He leaned a little toward her, and she did not move away, and the world narrowed to a space no wider than a breath. Then a voice like a foghorn boomed up from below, informing them that the biscuits had arrived and that somebody had better come and carry them before they went cold. Maren laughed until her ladder shook, and Felix climbed down with a face as red as a lantern.

Together they carried box after box of books down to the long tables along the shore and arranged them by subject, by colour and by whim, with a few promising surprises hidden at the bottom of each pile. Miss Pell added jars of autumn flowers, and soon every table looked like a small garden of stories waiting to be picked. The cafe woman set up her great steaming urns, and the smell of chocolate rolled over the water.

As the sun sank behind the mountains, the first coach rumbled into the lane and unloaded forty visitors in thick scarves and woollen hats, and soon afterwards a train from the city whistled in and poured out several hundred more. They stood blinking at the glowing lane as though they had walked into a story, and then they began to wander toward the water. Maren gripped the edge of the counter and whispered to Felix that it was really and truly happening at last.

One by one the lanterns were lit along the shore until the whole curve of the lake glowed gold from end to end, and the dark water doubled every flame until the town seemed to float among stars. The crowd, which had been chattering and stamping its feet against the cold, fell quiet with wonder. Somewhere the fiddle began to play, and the Night of Lanterns had truly begun.

Standing behind the book tables with the crowd pressing eagerly around her, Maren was seized by a sudden dizziness, as though the whole enormous evening were about to fall on her shoulders. She reached for Felix's hand without thinking, and he held it firmly, telling her in a low voice that she had made all of this happen and that she was doing wonderfully. She breathed in slowly, then out again, and felt the dizziness drain away, and she began to smile at the crowd.

At eight o'clock the fiddler lowered his bow, and Maren rang a small brass bell to ask for silence, and the whole shore turned toward the little stage. Felix climbed up with the old book of the lighthouse keeper in his hands, lit only by a ring of paper lanterns, and looked out at five hundred faces. He had addressed parliaments and ambassadors, but never before had his knees trembled quite like this.

Felix began to read the story of the lighthouse keeper in a low, warm voice that carried over the water without the slightest effort, and the great crowd leaned forward as one person to listen. When the keeper climbed the long stairs and lit his lamp for the lost ships, no one made a sound, and even the lake seemed to wait. It was the story that Maren's father had loved, and Felix read it as if for him.

When Felix read the last line and closed the book, there was a moment of perfect silence, and then the whole shore erupted in applause that rolled across the lake and came back from the mountains. Maren stood at the back of the crowd with tears running down her face, and she did not wipe them away, because she was too happy to care. Mrs Kell was blowing her nose like a trumpet and pretending that it was the cold.

By ten o'clock a long, cheerful queue had formed along the shore, and every person in it was holding a book, a biscuit or both. Felix, who had not touched the till since the first week, now worked the stall with the speed of a conjuror, wrapping, counting and chatting without a single mistake. Maren whispered to him that she had never seen anything so remarkable in her life.

Before long the cash box was almost empty of small coins, and the queue was growing impatient, and for a moment Maren looked as if she might faint. Mrs Kell strode over from the biscuit stall, emptied her own apron pockets onto the table with a clatter and told Felix that this was what small change was for. He thanked her gravely, and for once she laughed out loud at one of his bows.

At the edge of the crowd, Nina Strand moved quietly among the stalls and the lanterns with her camera held high, capturing the glow on the water and the faces of the happy visitors. She also took a great many pictures of the shop's new assistant, who was far too busy to notice, and each time she looked at them she frowned a little deeper. She was beginning, slowly and with growing excitement, to remember exactly where she had seen that face before.

By midnight the Lantern Bookshop had sold nearly every book on its shelves, and the visitors were still queueing with armfuls of paperbacks and eager faces. When Maren counted the takings at last, with Felix holding the lamp, she realised that in a single night the shop had earned almost everything it owed the bank. She sat down on the floor of the shop and laughed and cried at the same time.

She worked out on the back of a paper bag that only a small sum still remained, and that Felix's new plan, with its second-hand corner and its lantern kits, would bring that in within a few weeks. For the first time in years she believed, truly and completely, that the Lantern Bookshop would survive. She looked at Felix as though he were a miracle that had walked in off the street.

At midnight Joss and a dozen children in life jackets rowed out in the little boats and set the floating lanterns on the water, where they drifted apart like a field of small gold stars. The whole town stood on the shore in a hush of wonder, watching them turn slowly toward the far side of the lake. Even Mrs Kell, standing with her arms folded, was seen to wipe one eye with the corner of her apron.

At last the crowds drifted away to their coaches and their trains, and the town grew quiet, and the lanterns above the shore burned low and sleepy. Maren took Felix by the hand without a word and led him down the path to the little wooden bridge at the end of the lake. The water beneath them was full of drifting gold, and neither of them wanted the night to finish.

On the bridge Maren turned to him and thanked him, in a voice that shook a little, for everything he had done for her and for the shop and for her father's memory. Then, because there was nothing more to say, and because she had been wanting to for a very long time, she rose on her toes and kissed him. The lanterns drifted all around them on the dark water, like a hundred small and watchful moons keeping a secret.

They walked home slowly through the sleeping lane, hand in hand, saying nothing at all because nothing needed to be said. Pepper was waiting on the doorstep with her tail curled around her paws, and she looked at them both with the smug expression of a cat who has predicted everything. Felix felt that he could have walked like that to the other side of the world.

In the attic Felix lay awake and smiled at the dark ceiling for a very long time, until the cold thought crept in that the Harvest Ball was now less than two weeks away. His happiness turned to ice in his chest, because he knew that he had given Maren a kiss, a festival and a friendship, but not yet his real name. He resolved to tell her the whole truth at breakfast, and, because he was so afraid of it, he did not sleep at all.

They ate their breakfast together on the shop steps in the pale morning sun, with the lake glittering behind them and the last lanterns still swaying overhead, and Maren looked happier than he had ever seen her. She asked him, a little shyly and very bravely, whether he would consider staying in Lindenmere for good, as her partner in the shop and in everything else. It was the question he had dreamed of hearing, and it arrived at the worst possible moment.

Felix opened his mouth to say yes, and then to tell her the truth, and he discovered that he could do neither, because the one would be a betrayal and the other might be the end of everything. The lie sat between them on the step like an unwelcome guest, and the sunshine suddenly seemed too bright. He said that he would like nothing better, which was true, and added that there was something he needed to explain, which was worse.

Before he could say another word, Mrs Kell came hurrying across the lane with a folded newspaper clutched in her floury hand and a face as pale as her own dough. She was not a woman who hurried, and she was not a woman who was ever afraid, and the sight of both together made Felix's stomach turn over. She put the newspaper on the counter in silence and went to stand beside Maren.

The front page of the Brinmark Gazette carried a large photograph of Felix laughing at the postcard rack and, above it, a headline asking whether the missing Crown Prince of Aldoria had been found working in a Lindenmere bookshop. Beneath it a long article described the festival, the shop and the debt, and the prince's face stared out of every column. Somewhere in the city, a very pleased editor had sold a great many copies.

Maren read the headline twice, then read it a third time as though the words might rearrange themselves into something kinder, and slowly she raised her eyes to his face. Her hands were shaking so badly that the paper rattled, and her voice, when she spoke, was so quiet that he had to lean forward to hear. She asked him whether it was true, and she begged him with her eyes to say no.

Felix could not lie to her any longer, and the truth came out of him in a long, tumbling rush that he had rehearsed a hundred times and now could not order at all. He told her about the palace and the king, the engagement and the Harvest Ball, the night train, the name Fen and the sister who had pressed a coat into his hands. When he reached the end, the shop was so quiet that he could hear the clock.

Maren listened without moving, her arms folded tightly as if to keep her heart from escaping, and said nothing until he had finished. Then she told him that he had sat beside her and listened to all her fears while he kept the biggest secret of all. She said that she felt like a fool, and that the worst thing was not the lie but how much she had wanted to believe it.

Felix told her, in a voice that cracked, that he had been afraid that if she knew who he was she would see only a crown and a palace and never the man behind them. In Lindenmere, for the first time in his life, people had liked him for the things that he did, the stories he read and the soup that he burned, and he could not bear to lose that. He admitted that fear was no excuse for deceit, and that he knew it better than anyone could ever tell her.

Maren was crying now, quietly and without moving, and she said that she did not know who he was and that perhaps he did not know either. She asked him to return to his palace and his father and decide, once and for all, who he truly wished to be, because she could never trust a person who had not yet found himself. Then she pointed to the green door, and it was the hardest thing she had ever done.

Felix climbed to the attic and packed his small bag, which took no time at all, since he owned almost nothing, while Pepper sat on the bed and watched him with great round sorrowful eyes. He walked down through the silent shop, past the shelves he had learned and the counter where he had been happy, and out through the green door, which swung closed behind him with a small, final click. Behind it, in the shop that she had almost lost and almost saved, Maren sat down on the floor and wept.

At the end of the lane Captain Hale was waiting beside a long black car, standing as straight as a post and holding his cap against his chest. He was a kind old soldier who had known Felix since the prince was a small boy with a toy sword, and he did not say a single word of blame. He said only that the king was asking for him, and that the road home was a long one.

Nina Strand was standing nervously beside the car with her camera hanging limp at her side and an expression of real misery on her face. She told Felix that she had been about to ask for his side of the story when her editor, who had seen the photographs, printed the article without her consent, and that she was truly sorry for the pain. He told her, with a tired smile, that a secret could not be kept for ever.

Mrs Kell came marching down the lane with her apron flapping and pushed a warm paper bag of bread and star-shaped biscuits into his hands without a word of greeting. She told him gruffly that no boy, prince or otherwise, should travel on an empty stomach, and that he should come back when he had sorted himself out and not before. Then she turned on her heel and marched back up the lane, so that he would not see the expression on her face.

The children of the story hour had gathered in a silent row at the end of the lane, and little Ada stepped forward and held out a lopsided paper lantern that she had made herself. She told him very seriously that it would help him to find his way back, and that he was not to lose it. Felix knelt down on the cold cobbles to take it from her, and found that he could not speak a single word.

As the car pulled away from the kerb, Felix twisted around and looked back through the rear window at the faded ribbons of lanterns that still swayed across the lane, and at the green door that had stayed firmly shut. The lake shone behind them like a mirror, and then the road curved, and the whole bright town vanished behind a hill. He held Ada's little lantern in his lap with both hands, as carefully as if it were still alight, all the way to the mountains.

Captain Hale drove for a long time in silence along the winding road beside the railway, and at last, without taking his eyes from the road, he remarked that the king had hardly slept since the prince had gone. A father who shouts, he said, is very often a father who is frightened, and the king had never learned any other way to say so. Felix looked out of the window at the passing fields and said nothing, but he thought about it for a long time.

Hale said, with the shy smile of an old soldier unused to such talk, that he had understood at once why the prince had chosen the name Fen, for he still remembered the queen calling it across the palace gardens. The king had remembered it too, he added, and it had shaken him more than any report. Felix pressed his forehead against the cold glass and let the tears come at last.

By late afternoon the great white mountains of Aldoria rose in front of them, enormous and clean and glittering in the thin light, and the car began to climb through forests of dark pine. Felix felt fear and relief in exactly equal measure, as though his heart had been divided, and he could not tell which half would win. The air through the open window smelled of snow, and of every Christmas of his childhood.

It was fully dark when the car swept through the great gates of Halden Palace, and the servants lined up along the marble steps to bow, exactly as if nothing had happened. Felix felt the familiar walls close around him with a heavy and almost physical weight, and for a moment he wanted to turn and run back down the mountain. Then a small figure in a nightgown came flying down the steps, and Livia threw her arms around his neck.

Livia held on to her brother for a very long time, not caring who saw, and told him in a muffled voice that she had missed him dreadfully and that the palace had been horribly dull without him. She whispered that the king would see him in the great hall in the morning, in front of the whole court, and that Cecile had already arrived and was waiting in the library. Felix kissed the top of her head, squared his shoulders and walked up the steps and into the palace that he had left.

The next morning Felix walked the length of the great hall under the gaze of two hundred courtiers who had been told to look the other way and were looking at nothing else. King Anton sat on his high carved throne with his hands on his knees, as grey and hard as the stones of the palace, and he did not smile. Felix halted before the throne, bowed exactly as he had been taught as a boy, and waited for whatever was about to come.

The king did not ask where his son had been or why he had gone, and he made no mention of apologies or explanations or anything else that was human. He said only, in the cold, clear voice that he used for proclamations, that the engagement would be announced at the Harvest Ball exactly as planned, and that the matter was closed. A murmur ran through the watching court like wind through a field of dry grass, and then it died away.

Felix lifted his head, and in front of the entire court, for the first time in twenty-six years, he heard himself say no. The word rang through the great hall like a dropped bell, and every courtier drew in a breath so sharply that the candles seemed to flicker. He expected the roof to fall in, and instead there was only a silence so deep that he could hear his own pulse.

The king rose from his throne, cleared the hall with a single movement of his hand and led his son to a tall window overlooking the gardens, where the sun was setting in a haze of gold. A prince, he said stiffly, with his back turned, serves his people and the crown, and it is not for him to choose his own path. His voice sounded older than Felix remembered it, and a good deal less certain than the words that it spoke.

Felix answered quietly, and without a trace of anger, that a prince who is never allowed to choose is nothing but a costume that is carried from room to room, and that a kingdom deserves something more than a costume. If he was to serve his people honestly, he said, he must first be permitted to decide how, and whom he would love. The king did not reply to this at once, but Felix saw that his hands, which had been clenched, slowly unclenched.

At last the king told his son that the Harvest Ball would take place in just over a week, and that Felix should go to his rooms and think very carefully about what he had said. It was neither agreement nor refusal, and it was the longest conversation the two of them had had in ten years. Felix bowed and left the room with his back straight, and it was only in the corridor that his legs began to tremble.

That night Felix, Livia and Lady Cecile met in the library behind a locked door and whispered together by the light of a single candle, like conspirators in an old adventure. Cecile thanked Felix for his courage, which he said he did not possess, and together the three of them made a plan to refuse the engagement in front of the whole court. Livia took notes in a small blue book with the severity of a general.

Cecile told Felix about Tomas Brandt, the stable master, who had taught her to ride when she was nine and had never said a word of love until the day she asked him to, and her face shone. She would speak first at the ball, she decided, and Felix would stand up and agree with her, so that neither of them would face the king alone. Felix promised her, with his hand upon his heart, that he would stand beside her faithfully to the very end.

Late that night Felix sat at his desk, surrounded by crumpled paper, and began a letter to Maren that he rewrote nine times, throwing away each draft because every sentence sounded like an excuse or a speech. In the end he wrote only a few short lines, which were honest and plain, and he did not read them over for fear of tearing them up. He folded the note into a small parcel, together with something that he had found in the library.

In a dusty corner of the library he had found his mother's own worn copy of The Lamplighter's Daughter, with her name written in a girlish hand inside the cover and a pressed flower marking the last page. He wrapped it as carefully as a jewel, and Captain Hale, who asked no questions, sent it by the fastest rider to Lindenmere that very morning. After that there was nothing left for Felix to do except wait, and he found that waiting was the hardest task of all.

A few days later a small brown parcel arrived for Maren, delivered by a mud-spattered rider who had come down from the mountains and who refused to say a word about where he had been. She opened it slowly at the counter, with Pepper looking on and Mrs Kell hovering in the doorway pretending to read the notices. Inside lay something wrapped carefully in blue tissue paper, and beside it a small folded note with her name on the front.

Inside the tissue paper lay a very old copy of The Lamplighter's Daughter, the very book that her father had loved and read aloud so many times, with a cover soft with handling. A woman's name was written in the front, and a dried flower was pressed between the last pages. Maren sat down slowly on the stool, holding it against her chest, and for a long time she could not speak.

The note was short and plain and written in a hand that seemed to have trembled. It said that the book had belonged to his mother, who had read it to him when he was small, and that he hoped to become a man who could read it aloud to Maren without a mask. It was signed Felix, called Fen, and there was a blot where a tear had fallen.

That night Maren sat alone in the sleeping shop and read the first chapter of the old book by the light of a single lamp, turning the pages with great care, like someone handling a bird. She could almost hear her father's warm voice reading the words, and for the first time since the funeral she wept for him freely, without hurry or shame. Somewhere in that long evening, she understood how much it had cost Felix to send it.

In the morning she was angry again, and she informed Pepper, who was sitting on the open book in a posture of great judgement, that a person who has lied cannot be forgiven with a single present. Pepper stared at her with unblinking green eyes, as if to point out that she had read the book all night, and Maren was at last forced to laugh. It was a very uncomfortable and slightly humbling thing, she reflected, to be understood so completely by a cat.

A few days later a thick cream-coloured card arrived from Princess Livia, inviting Miss Maren Vos to the Harvest Ball at Halden Palace and promising, in a hasty postscript at the bottom, that the journey would be worth every mile. It smelled faintly of lavender and, more distantly, of apple pie, and the handwriting was as bold as a flag. Maren held it at arm's length as though it might bite her, and then she held it a little closer.

Maren almost threw the card into the stove, but Mrs Kell, who had come in to borrow a book and read it, informed her in no uncertain terms that she was going and that there would be no discussion. A person who has read half a story, she declared, has a duty to see how it ends, and Maren Vos was no coward. Maren opened her mouth to object, and to her own great surprise she found that she had no objections left at all.

Mrs Kell, who had learned to sew as a girl and never told a soul, found a length of deep green silk in her attic and stitched a gown for Maren in four sleepless nights. Miss Pell contributed a ribbon, Mr Ferris a silver buckle and Joss a pair of borrowed shoes, and by the end of the week half the town had added something to the outfit. It was, by a very long way, the most beautiful thing that Maren had ever put on in the whole of her life.

The town promised to run the shop while she was away, and Mr Ferris and Joss climbed onto the roof with hammers to mend the leak that had troubled the Lantern Bookshop for years. That night Maren boarded the train to Aldoria in her green dress, with the old book in her bag, and watched the mountains rise black and enormous against the stars. She had no idea what she would say, or whether she would say anything at all.

Captain Hale met her at the little station with a gleaming car and bowed as though she were a duchess, which left her more flustered than any speech could have done. When they reached Halden Palace, Livia ran down the steps to meet her and led her through a series of glittering corridors to a quiet corner beside the great ballroom doors. She whispered to wait there, and to watch, and that she should listen for her cue.

The Harvest Ball glittered in the Hall of Mirrors, where hundreds of dancers in silk and velvet swirled beneath chandeliers that blazed like a hundred small suns. At the height of the music King Anton rose, raised his hand, and the orchestra stopped in the middle of a bar, and a hush spread over the room. Everyone in the glittering room knew what he was about to announce, and almost everyone, as it turned out, was quite mistaken.

Before the king could utter a word, Lady Cecile Marchand stepped forward in her pale blue gown, her chin high and her hands perfectly steady, and addressed the astonished court. She said, in a clear and carrying voice, that she had the greatest respect for the prince and the crown, but that she would not marry a man she did not love. A gasp went round the great room like a wave breaking, and then nobody dared to breathe at all.

Then she turned and held out her hand toward the edge of the crowd, where Tomas Brandt stood stiff in his best coat, pale as paper, with his cap crushed between his fingers. He came forward through the whispering guests as though walking into a storm, took her hand and walked beside her to the doors, and they did not look back. It was, the old courtiers whispered afterwards, the bravest thing that the court of Aldoria had seen in a hundred years.

The king's face turned to stone, and the whole court waited in terror to see what thunderbolt he would hurl. Then Felix stepped forward into the empty space in the middle of the floor, with his heart hammering, and declared in a voice that surprised everyone that he agreed with every word that Lady Cecile had said. Somewhere near the doors, Livia pressed both of her hands over her mouth to keep from cheering.

Felix told the court that he would serve his country all the days of his life, but in his own way, by building a library in every mountain village and giving every child in Aldoria a book to hold. He added that when he married it would be for love and for nothing else, and that a kingdom whose prince had never been allowed to choose could not expect him to lead it with an open heart. He had never in his whole life spoken so plainly or so freely before, and he found that he rather liked it.

There was a long and dreadful silence, and then, from the edge of the room, a single pair of hands began to clap, loudly and without the slightest hesitation. It was Livia, who had climbed onto a gilded chair to make sure she was seen, and one by one the courtiers followed her, until half the hall was applauding and the other half was too astonished to stop them. Even old Captain Hale, standing stiffly beside the door with his cap under his arm, was seen to clap his hands.

Over the heads of the applauding crowd, Felix saw a woman in a green dress standing alone in the great doorway, with an old book clasped to her chest and a look of wonder on her face. He forgot the court, the king and the crown, and crossed the entire length of the Hall of Mirrors as if the floor were a bridge and the world had fallen away on either side. Two hundred guests in silks and jewels moved aside for him without a word, as the sea might part for a ship.

Felix stopped before her and said, a little breathlessly, that he was Felix and also Fen, that he was sorry for every lie, and that he wanted to learn to be one honest man for the rest of his life. Maren held up the old book and said that she had read all of it, and that she thought he had already begun. Then, in front of the entire court of Aldoria and the king himself, with the old book still held between them, she kissed him.

King Anton watched his son and the bookseller from across the long hall, and slowly the stern lines of his face began to soften, like ice in the first warm wind of spring. He remembered a crowded market square, a summer morning, and a girl with flour on her cheek who had sold him an apple pie and refused to call him sir. He had been a frightened young prince once, and a girl had been brave for him, and he had somehow forgotten.

Months later, the first of Felix's village libraries had opened in Aldoria, paid for by the Royal Reading Fund that he and Livia had founded. Every Saturday the prince himself arrived in Lindenmere in an old cap to read to the children, while the Lantern Bookshop filled with readers and the bank was repaid in full. A new sign over the green door welcomed readers of every kind, and Maren took his hand, understanding that some stories end well because someone was brave enough to begin.
